additions.title: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058
additions.locator: Ground 3, paras 145 to 154; quote at para 153; order, para 1
additions.quote: the DPIA failed properly to assess the risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects
additions.why: The leading UK judgment on what makes an impact assessment inadequate. The police force had written one for live facial recognition, and the lower court accepted it; the Court of Appeal held it deficient. The assessment proceeded on the footing that privacy rights were not infringed, when the court had found the rules left too much discretion over who went on watchlists and where cameras were used; so it had not properly assessed the risks or the measures to address them. An assessment that exists can still fail. Limits: decided under section 64 of the Data Protection Act 2018 (law enforcement processing), not UK GDPR Article 35, though the required contents are closely similar; a 2020 judgment on one force's trials.

additions.title: Data Protection Act 2018, section 64: Data protection impact assessment
additions.quote: the controller must, prior to the processing, carry out a data protection impact assessment
additions.why: The duty the court applied in Bridges: for law enforcement processing likely to result in high risk, an assessment before processing that covers the operations, the risks to people, the measures to address them and the safeguards. Shows the 'before, not after' rule is statute in both UK regimes. Limits: Part 3 only (competent authorities processing for law enforcement purposes). In force 25 May 2018; no amendment notes on the section.

additions.title: UK GDPR, Article 36: Prior consultation
additions.quote: would result in a high risk in the absence of measures taken by the controller to mitigate the risk
additions.why: The consequence of an honest assessment: if it shows a high risk that the controller's measures do not reduce, the regulator must be consulted before processing starts, and may give written advice within eight weeks, extendable by six. This is what 'acted on' means at the top of the scale. Limits: the text now reads 'the Commission' following the change of regulator; how often prior consultation is used in practice was not found.

additions.title: Age appropriate design: a code of practice for online services. 2. Data protection impact assessments
additions.locator: Standard 2, opening statement and 'What do you mean by a DPIA?'; 'When do we need to do a DPIA?'
additions.quote: You should begin a DPIA early in the design of your service, before you start your processing.
additions.why: A statutory code of practice that makes the impact assessment its second standard for any online service children are likely to use; a consumer AI product that children are likely to use would be in scope. It requires a new assessment before significant changes to an existing service and says outside events, such as a new public concern, may prompt a review. Limits: applies to online services likely to be accessed by children; the page prints no date (page metadata 17 December 2025, used for the year); the date the code was issued is not shown on this page.

additions.title: Reprimand: Chelmer Valley High School
additions.quote: no DPIA had been completed for the introduction of facial recognition technology prior to the processing commencing in March 2023
additions.why: A UK enforcement outcome where the formal finding is a breach of Article 35(1) itself, which the first research pass did not find. A school brought in facial recognition for about 1,200 pupils in March 2023 and completed its assessment in November 2023; the regulator said an assessment done first would have exposed the consent failures that followed. Limits: a reprimand to a school, with no fine; biometric recognition, not a decision-making system; filed under 'regulator guidance' because the type list has no value for enforcement action. The 22 July 2024 date is from the regulator's enforcement page; the PDF file name carries 2 July.

additions.title: Carrying out a data protection impact assessment if necessary (AI how-to sheets)
additions.publisher: Commission Nationale de l'Informatique et des Libertés (CNIL)
additions.locator: Introduction and section 'The realisation of a DPIA for the development of AI systems'
additions.quote: should be changed iteratively as the characteristics of the processing and risk assessment evolve
additions.why: AI-specific guidance on impact assessments from a major European regulator. It says building a training dataset can itself create high risk, applies the two-criteria screening rule to AI development, and deals with the case where the developer cannot foresee the deployed use: the developer assesses development and the deploying organisation completes the picture. Supports the 'currency' level of the criterion. Limits: French regulator, EU GDPR; a courtesy translation, with the French text prevailing. Not binding in the UK.

additions.title: Guide to undertaking privacy impact assessments
additions.publisher: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
additions.locator: Section 'When to do a PIA'; footnote 3 on the Australian Government Agencies Privacy Code
additions.quote: a PIA should be an integral part of the project planning process, not an afterthought
additions.why: International comparator. Australia requires an impact assessment by law only of government agencies running high privacy risk projects, yet the regulator's test of a good one is the same as the UK's: early enough to change the design or stop the project, and evolving with it. Limits: Australian law and terminology (privacy impact assessment); guidance, not a binding rule for private organisations.

additions.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
additions.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
additions.quote: Impacts to individuals, groups, communities, organizations, and society are characterized.
additions.why: The only free standard found that covers impact assessment for AI; the ISO impact-assessment standards are sold and their catalogue page blocked a plain request in the first pass. MAP 5.1 asks for the likelihood and size of each impact to be identified and documented, drawing on past incidents and outside feedback. Wider than a data protection assessment: it looks beyond personal data. Limits: voluntary United States framework, not UK law, and not a substitute for the Article 35 assessment.

additions.title: Fairness and Data Protection Impact Assessments
additions.publisher: Atoosa Kasirzadeh and Damian Clifford, AIES '21: Proceedings of the 2021 AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (authors' copy on arXiv)
additions.quote: they rarely mention the fairness principle in practice
additions.why: Peer-reviewed analysis of regulators' guidance on impact assessments. Finds that although fairness should have a large place in the assessment, the guidance documents seldom mention it. Supports testing depth, not only existence: an assessment can follow the guidance and still miss whether the system treats people fairly. Limits: a review of guidance documents under the EU GDPR as they stood in 2021, not a study of assessments organisations have written; only the abstract is on the linked page.

additions.title: An Institutional View of Algorithmic Impact Assessments
additions.publisher: Andrew D. Selbst, Harvard Journal of Law & Technology vol. 35 no. 1
additions.locator: Abstract, p. 117 of the volume (first page of the PDF)
additions.quote: It is therefore inevitable that technology firms will have an amount of practical discretion in the assessment
additions.why: Explains why impact assessments drift into paperwork: only the firm holds the knowledge needed, so it has wide discretion, and commercial incentives shape how it is used. Argues rules must be designed with that in mind. The best account found of the gap between the criterion's second and third levels. Limits: a United States law review article (student-edited), about proposed algorithmic impact assessments in the US, not the UK duty; argument drawing on organisational research, not new data.

additions.title: Towards An Automated AI Act FRIA Tool That Can Reuse GDPR's DPIA
additions.publisher: Tytti Rintamaki and Harshvardhan J. Pandit, arXiv (presented at the CLAIRvoyant workshop 2024)
additions.quote: align the two to state where a DPIA can be reused in a FRIA
additions.why: Bears on the top level of the criterion, reuse of the assessment as evidence. Maps the information in a data protection impact assessment against the EU AI Act's fundamental rights impact assessment to show which parts carry over. Limits: a workshop paper on arXiv, not journal peer reviewed; EU law only; written before the 2026 changes to the AI Act, which amended the paragraph on reuse; only the abstract is on the linked page.

rejected.title: Zarrabi, Wagner and Boiten, Changes in Conducting Data Protection Risk Assessment: Before and After GDPR implementation
rejected.reason: Read. UK authors; two focus groups, ten privacy professionals. Would have been the UK-sample study, but it is an unreviewed preprint, the findings are thin, and the PDF text extracts with broken words so no exact quote could be relied on. Not kept.

rejected.title: Kaminski and Malgieri, 'Algorithmic impact assessments under the GDPR: producing multi-layered explanations', International Data Privacy Law 11(2), 2021
rejected.reason: Blocked: HTTP 403 (browser challenge) on the publisher's page. Not read, not cited.

rejected.title: Algorithmic Impact Assessment tool and Directive on Automated Decision-Making (Canada)
rejected.reason: Blocked: HTTP 403. Not read, not cited.

rejected.title: Council of Europe, HUDERIA methodology for risk and impact assessment of AI systems
rejected.reason: Not read: the Council of Europe document server returned HTTP 403 to a plain request (tested on the Framework Convention text).

rejected.title: ISO/IEC 29134 and ISO/IEC 42005 (impact assessment standards)
rejected.reason: Paid standards; the ISO catalogue page returned HTTP 403 in the first pass. Not retried, not cited.

rejected.reason: Not searched for: the Chelmer Valley reprimand already supplies a formal Article 35 finding.

brief_check: Nothing read contradicts the approved brief. One gap it can now close: the research log said no enforcement case with a formal Article 35 finding had been confirmed; the Chelmer Valley High School reprimand (July 2024) is one, and Bridges (Court of Appeal, 2020) is a judgment holding an assessment inadequate under the parallel law enforcement duty.
